A 78-year-old male presents for a routine health maintenance visit. He reports feeling well overall,
aside from occasional lower back pain over the past few years. He has a history of a right-sided
myocardial infarction 4 years ago and currently denies any shortness of breath or chest pain. He
previously smoked one pack of cigarettes daily but quit 10 years ago and does not consume alcohol.
His vital signs include a pulse of 44/min and blood pressure of 142/82 mm Hg. Physical examination
reveals 1+ lower extremity edema, with no abnormalities noted on cardiac or pulmonary examination.
There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory results are as follows: | Hemoglobin | 13.5
g/dL | | --- | --- | | Leukocyte count | 6500/mm³ | | Platelet count | 210,000/mm³ | | Serum | | | Na■ | 140
mEq/L | | K■ | 4.2 mEq/L | | Ca²■ | 10.1 mg/dL | | Protein | 9.8 g/dL | | Creatinine | 1.0 mg/dL | An ECG
shows persistent Q-wave abnormalities consistent with prior findings from one year ago. Serum protein
electrophoresis reveals a monoclonal spike in the gamma region, and immunofixation identifies
overproduction of IgG and kappa light chains, with a normal kappa-to-lambda free light chain ratio.
What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step? Answer Choices: (A) Bone marrow aspiration and
biopsy (B) Flow cytometry of peripheral blood (C) Serum beta-2 microglobulin (D) Urine dipstick (E)
